cases.title: Integrated Case 1 — Kaveri Appliances Ltd. (external scan to competitive position)
facts: Kaveri Appliances Ltd. makes domestic water purifiers in Coimbatore and sells across four southern states. Its strategy team is preparing a three-year plan and has gathered the following facts.

**Macro facts.** The State has announced a 15% capital subsidy for appliance manufacturing and has tightened e-waste rules, which will require Kaveri to fund a take-back scheme. Bank lending rates have risen by 150 basis points. Census data for the four states shows a rising share of households in the 25–40 age band with monthly incomes above ₹60,000. Public concern about plastic waste has grown sharply, and three competitors have been criticised in the press for non-recyclable filter cartridges. A new low-cost UV-LED purification module has become commercially available.

**Industry facts.** Four firms, including Kaveri, hold roughly equal shares of the branded southern market; none can dictate price. All four assemble in leased plants with heavy annual lease and staff commitments. Two large e-commerce platforms account for 48% of Kaveri's sales and press annually for deeper discounts. The single supplier of the membrane used in Kaveri's premium range holds the relevant patent and has raised prices twice this year. Packaged drinking-water home delivery is spreading rapidly in the same cities at a lower monthly cost than owning a purifier.

**Competitor facts.** AquaNeat sells only through its own service franchisees, carries the widest range, charges a premium and is nationally known. ValuePure sells a narrow two-model range at the lowest price through all channels, with no installation service. PureLife matches Kaveri on price and range but its published accounts show interest cover below 1.5 and its online reviews complain repeatedly about delayed service visits.

**Kaveri's own facts.** Its oldest gravity-filter line has had falling sales and profits for three years as RO models replaced it. Its mid-price RO range has grown fast for two years, with prices softening as rivals copied it. Its new UV-LED model has just been launched: few customers know of it, the price is high and no rival offers one. Cumulative output of the mid-price range has quadrupled in four years and its cost per unit has fallen 22% over the same period, from retraining, a redesigned housing, a larger moulding press and automated leak-testing.

questions.q: Classify Kaveri's three product lines by product-life-cycle stage, and state the strategic choice the study material attaches to each.

options.A: Gravity filter in maturity, RO range in decline, UV-LED in growth — harvest all three
options.B: Gravity filter in decline, RO range in growth, UV-LED in introduction — selective harvesting or retrenchment for the first, expansion for the other two
options.C: All three in maturity — maintain stability across the portfolio
options.D: Gravity filter in introduction, RO range in maturity, UV-LED in growth — invest in the first two only

reasoning: **Gravity filter — decline:** 'sharp downward drift in sales… some new product replaces the existing product' (SM §2.4.1). RO models replacing it is the textbook cause. A combination of strategies — diversification or retrenchment, and in portfolio terms selective harvesting — applies.
**Mid-price RO — growth:** 'the demand expands rapidly, prices fall, competition increases and market expands'. Prices softening as rivals copy is the growth signature, not maturity.

**UV-LED — introduction:** 'slow sales growth, competition is almost negligible, prices are relatively high, and markets are limited… lack of awareness on the part of customers'. All four conditions are present.

**Strategic choice by stage:** expansion is feasible for introductory and growth businesses; mature businesses are cash sources; selective harvesting and retrenchment suit declining ones. The main advantage of the PLC approach is exactly this diagnosis of a portfolio.

questions.q: Using Porter's Five Forces, which single force is Kaveri's **supplier** problem, and which force does the spread of packaged water home delivery represent?

options.A: Both are supplier bargaining power, because both concern inputs
options.B: The membrane supplier is rivalry; packaged water is a new entrant
options.C: The membrane supplier is supplier bargaining power; packaged water home delivery is the threat of substitutes
options.D: The membrane supplier is a barrier to entry; packaged water is buyer bargaining power

reasoning: **Supplier power:** suppliers command bargaining power when 'their products are crucial to the buyer and substitutes are not available', when they 'can erect high switching costs' and when they are 'more concentrated than their buyers' (SM §2.5.1). A sole patented membrane supplier meets all three, and supplier power 'determines the cost of raw materials and other inputs… and therefore industry attractiveness and profitability'.

**Substitutes:** 'Substitute products offering a price advantage and/or performance improvement to the consumer can drastically alter the competitive character of an industry. And they can bring it about all of a sudden.' The test is a product that performs 'the same, or nearly the same, function' — delivered drinking water performs the purifier's function at lower monthly cost, and comes from a different industry.

ICAI's own parallel: coir suffered at the hands of synthetic fibre; and real estate, insurance, bonds and bank deposits are substitutes for common stocks because they are alternate ways to invest funds.

Note that the e-commerce platforms taking 48% of sales and pressing for discounts are a third, separate force: buyer bargaining power, since they 'spend a lot of money on the industry's products, i.e. they are big buyers'.

questions.q: Kaveri's four equal rivals, their heavy lease and staff commitments, and the absence of product differences point to which published conditions, and with what consequence?

options.A: High exit barriers alone, which raise industry profitability
options.B: A strong industry leader disciplining price wars, which protects margins
options.C: Slow growth alone, which is temporary and self-correcting
options.D: Number of competitors, high fixed costs and lack of product differentiation — three of the six conditions of cut-throat rivalry, which lower profitability for all

reasoning: **Number of competitors:** with four roughly equal firms and no leader, 'the leader's ability to exert pricing discipline diminishes with the increased number of rivals', and no single firm can control pricing.

**High fixed costs:** 'when rivals operate with high fixed costs, they feel strong motivation to utilize their capacity and therefore are inclined to cut prices when they have excess capacity… profitability tends to be lower in industries characterized by high fixed costs'. Leases and staff commitments are exactly that.

**Lack of product differentiation:** 'firms can sometimes insulate themselves from price wars by differentiating their products… profitability tends to be lower in industries involving undifferentiated commodities'.

Option A inverts the rule: profitability tends to be **higher** in industries with **few** exit barriers, because rivalry declines when competitors can leave. Option B fails because the facts say no firm can dictate price, so there is no disciplining leader.

questions.q: Kaveri wants to position itself against AquaNeat, ValuePure and PureLife. Name the tool, the two variables it should plot, and the step at which PureLife's weakness enters the analysis.

options.A: Strategic group mapping; price/quality range and degree of service offered; PureLife's weakness enters at step (iv), determining the weaknesses of competitors
options.B: SWOT analysis; strengths and weaknesses; PureLife's weakness is a threat to Kaveri
options.C: BCG matrix; market growth and relative market share; PureLife is a dog
options.D: PESTLE analysis; legal and economic factors; PureLife's interest cover is an economic factor

reasoning: **The tool:** a strategic group consists of rival firms with similar competitive approaches and positions in the market, and strategic group mapping identifies those positions (SM §2.7.1). ICAI recommends it whenever a case asks for the market position of rivals — PYQ Jan 2026 Q5(a), MTP Mar 2024 S1 Q3(a), MTP May 2026 S1 Q1(a).

**The variables:** the six typical variables are price/quality range, geographic coverage, degree of vertical integration, product-line breadth, use of distribution channels and degree of service offered. The facts differentiate these four firms on price band and on service: AquaNeat is premium with franchised service, ValuePure is lowest price with no installation service, PureLife and Kaveri sit in the middle. Product-line breadth would serve equally well as the second variable.

**Where the weakness enters:** step (iv) of the competitive landscape — 'weaknesses (and strengths) can be identified by going through consumer reports and reviews appearing in various media', and 'financial strength and weakness can always be learnt from annual reports'. PureLife's delayed-service reviews and sub-1.5 interest cover are both named sources.

**Step (v) then does the work:** put all the information together, draw an inference about what rivals are **not** offering and what Kaveri can do to fill the gap — here, a mid-price model with reliable service and a recyclable cartridge, aimed at the group PureLife is failing.

cases.takeaway: One case can demand four different lists — the PLC stages, the five forces, the six conditions of rivalry and the competitive-landscape steps with strategic group mapping. The discipline that earns the marks is naming which list the sub-question wants before writing a word of it.

cases.title: Integrated Case 2 — Nalanda Learning Ltd. (macro scan, customer behaviour and key success factors)
facts: Nalanda Learning Ltd. sells examination-preparation courses in India and is considering its first overseas venture.

**The macro scan.** A new education regulation will require every online provider to register and file quarterly data. GST on digital services may be revised. Household spending on coaching in Tier-2 cities has risen with incomes, while the share of 18–24 year-olds in the population is at its peak. Parents increasingly judge providers by placement outcomes rather than by the number of lectures. Generative-AI tutors have appeared and three start-ups now offer unlimited AI doubt-solving at a tenth of Nalanda's fee. Nalanda's own servers consume a large amount of power and it has been asked to publish its energy usage.

**The overseas plan.** Nalanda first mapped global demand for Indian-curriculum coaching and currency and regulatory trends; then narrowed to the Gulf region, where a large expatriate Indian population and strong purchasing power make demand likely; then studied the United Arab Emirates in detail — its education licensing rules, corporate tax, data-residency law and the local preference for in-person revision classes — before deciding between a franchise and a wholly owned centre.

**Customer facts.** A buyer survey found that the fee is almost always paid by a parent while the course is used by the student. Enrolment spikes after a topper's video testimonial is circulated on social media. Students who enrol say they first recognised they were behind in a subject, then listed three or four providers, then compared syllabus coverage, faculty and price before choosing. Those who passed renewed for the next level and recommended Nalanda to juniors; those who failed did neither and said so publicly.

**Industry facts.** Across the coaching industry, students choose almost entirely on faculty reputation and on published results; costs per enrolled student fall steeply as a batch fills, because faculty cost is fixed; and the providers that last are those whose brand is trusted by parents. Nalanda's strategy head has drafted a list of eleven 'key success factors' for the board, including office décor and the number of social-media posts per week.

questions.q: Classify Nalanda's six macro facts into the PESTLE heads.

options.A: Registration rules — legal; GST revision — economic; rising Tier-2 spending and the 18–24 peak — socio-cultural and demographic (Social under PESTLE); outcome-based judgement — social; AI tutors — technological; energy disclosure — environmental
options.B: All six are political, since each involves a rule or a trend
options.C: Registration rules — political; AI tutors — legal; energy disclosure — economic; the rest — social
options.D: Registration and GST — legal; AI and energy — technological; the rest cannot be classified

reasoning: **Legal factors** 'affect how a company operates, its costs, and the demand for its products, ease of business' — a registration and quarterly-filing obligation is squarely legal (SM §2.3.3).

**Economic factors:** tax policy sits in the political head in the drivers table ('current and future taxation policy') and GST on services also changes price and demand; ICAI's PESTLE answers treat tax as political and the demand consequence as economic. Either attribution earns the mark provided the reasoning is given — but rising household spending and purchasing power is unambiguously economic.

**Social (socio-cultural) and demographic:** the 18–24 share is a population *characteristic* (demographic environment, §2.3.2) while the shift to judging providers by placement outcomes is a change in *attitudes* (socio-cultural). Under PESTLE both fall in the 'S' head, whose drivers include lifestyle trends, demographics, consumer attitudes and opinions, and consumer buying patterns.

**Technological:** AI tutors are the study material's own example of a technology that is simultaneously opportunity and threat, 'making obsolete most of the existing business products and services'. **Environmental:** energy consumption and waste disposal are named drivers under the environmental head.

questions.q: The three-stage overseas scan Nalanda ran corresponds to which published framework?

options.A: The three strategic levels — corporate, business and functional
options.B: The three levels of international environmental assessment — multinational, regional and country
options.C: The three steps of using Porter's Five Forces
options.D: The three issues to consider for strategic analysis

reasoning: **Multinational environmental analysis** 'involves identifying, anticipating, and monitoring significant components of the global environment on a large scale', including governments' free or interventionist tendencies — Nalanda's first stage.

**Regional environmental analysis** is 'a more in-depth evaluation of the critical factors in a specific geographical area', emphasising 'discovering market opportunities for a goods, services, or innovations in the chosen location' — the Gulf stage.

**Country environmental analysis** 'has to take a deeper look at the important environmental factors. Study of economic, legal, political, and cultural dimensions is required… customised for each of the countries to develop effective market entrance strategies' — the UAE stage, which is why the franchise-versus-own-centre choice belongs there.

An assessment of the external environment is 'the first step toward internationalisation', and the four steps of international strategic planning follow: evaluate global opportunities and threats against internal capabilities, describe the scope of operations, create global business objectives, develop distinct corporate strategies.

questions.q: On the customer facts, which pairing is correct?

options.A: The parent is the consumer and the student the customer; the testimonial is an internal influence; renewal is a decision-making stage
options.B: Both parent and student are customers; the testimonial is a post-decision process; failure is dissonance
options.C: The parent is the customer and the student the consumer; the testimonial is an external influence; the four-step comparison is the decision-making domain; renewal and public criticism are the post-decision processes
options.D: The distinction between customer and consumer does not apply to services

reasoning: **Customer versus consumer:** 'Customers are the purchasers of products and services in the economy, and they might exist as consumers or only as customers', while 'individuals or businesses that consume or utilise products and services are referred to as consumers' (SM §2.6.1). ICAI's own illustration is the parent who buys groceries consumed by the whole family — the same structure as a parent paying for a student's course.

**External influence:** external influences are 'like advertisement, peer recommendations or social norms', divided into 'the company's marketing efforts and the numerous environmental elements'. A circulated topper testimonial is both a marketing effort and a peer recommendation.

**Decision making:** the stated stages are problem recognition (realising they are behind), search for desirable alternatives and listing them (three or four providers), seeking information and weighing pros and cons (syllabus, faculty, price) and making a final choice. The study material adds that the full process 'mostly applies when the purchase is one that is significant to the customer' — a course that shapes a career qualifies.

**Post-decision processes:** 'a happy customer may make repeat purchase and recommend to others, customer with dissonance will neither purchase the product again nor recommend it to others'. Renewal and recommendation on one side, public criticism on the other.

questions.q: Advise the board on the strategy head's eleven-item KSF list.

options.A: Approve it; a longer list captures more of what matters
options.B: Reject the list and substitute Porter's five forces, since KSFs are not a published concept
options.C: Keep only the items that can be measured in rupees
options.D: Cut it to three or four — faculty reputation and published results (why customers choose), batch-fill cost efficiency (the resource and capability needed) and parental trust in the brand (what sustains advantage) — and resist the minor items

reasoning: The study material is explicit: 'Only rarely does an industry have more than three or four key success factors at any one time. And even among these three or four, one or two usually outrank the others in importance. Managers, therefore, have to resist the temptation to include factors that have only minor importance on their list.'

It goes further on the reason: 'To compile a list of every factor that matters even a little bit defeats the purpose of concentrating management attention on the factors truly critical to long-term competitive success.' Office décor and posts per week are exactly such minor items.

**The three identification questions produce the short list.** On what basis do customers choose between competing brands, and what product attributes are crucial to sales? — faculty reputation and published results. What resources and competitive capabilities does a seller need? — the cost efficiency that comes from filling batches against a fixed faculty cost. What does it take to achieve a sustainable competitive advantage? — parental trust in the brand, which the industry facts say determines which providers last.

**Then act on them:** 'an organisation with perceptive understanding of industry KSFs can gain sustainable competitive advantage by training its strategy on industry KSFs and devoting its energies to being distinctively better than rivals on one or more of these factors', while 'misdiagnosing the industry factors critical to long-term competitive success greatly raises the risk of a misdirected strategy'.

cases.takeaway: The 2026 edition's newer headings — market and customer, customer analysis, customer behaviour — are examined through exactly this kind of case. Note how the customer/consumer distinction, the four behavioural domains and the KSF cap each turn a plausible-sounding business decision into a specific published rule.

mcqs.question: The study material states two major limitations of strategic analysis. The second is that it:

options.A: Can be time-consuming, hurting overall organisational functioning and straining other efficient innovations
options.B: Cannot be applied to service businesses
options.C: Requires a formal environmental scanning department
options.D: Ignores the internal environment altogether

mcqs.explanation: SM §2.2: the first limitation is that it gives many options without telling which to pick; the second is that it can be time-consuming, hurting organisational functioning and straining other efficient innovations such as developing a new product or service.

mcqs.question: Within the micro environment, which of the following issues does the study material say a firm must address?

options.A: Inflation and the exchange rate
options.B: The ways in which the firm can raise its finance
options.C: The political ideology of the ruling party
options.D: International treaty and law

mcqs.explanation: SM §2.3.1 lists six micro-environment issues: the employees and how they are organised, the existing customer base, the ways the firm can raise finance, who the suppliers are and how the links are developed, the local community, and the direct competition and their comparative performance.

mcqs.question: 'Replacement technology/solutions', 'maturity of technology' and 'innovation potential' appear in the study material as drivers of change under which PESTLE head?

options.A: Economic
options.B: Legal
options.C: Environmental
options.D: Technological

mcqs.explanation: SM §2.3.3 drivers table, technological head: replacement technology/solutions; maturity of technology; manufacturing maturity and capacity; innovation potential; technology access, licensing, patents, property rights and copyrights.

mcqs.question: Which is the **second** step in international strategic planning?

options.A: Create the firm's global business objectives
options.B: Describe the scope of the firm's global commercial operations
options.C: Develop distinct corporate strategies for the global business and the whole organisation
options.D: Evaluate global opportunities and threats and rate them with internal capabilities

mcqs.explanation: SM §2.3.4: evaluate global opportunities and threats → describe the scope of operations → create global business objectives → develop distinct corporate strategies.

mcqs.question: A product feature is described in the study material as:

options.A: The physical packaging of the product
options.B: The warranty attached to the product
options.C: A component of a product that satisfies a consumer need
options.D: The margin the product earns over its cost

mcqs.explanation: SM §2.4: 'A product feature is a component of a product that satisfies a consumer need.' Features determine product pricing and are altered during development to optimise the user experience.

mcqs.question: In the growth stage of the product life cycle, as described in the study material:

options.A: Prices rise because demand exceeds supply
options.B: Competition remains almost negligible
options.C: Demand expands rapidly, prices fall, competition increases and the market expands
options.D: Profit falls because the market has stabilised

mcqs.explanation: SM §2.4.1: the growth stage has rapid market acceptance — demand expands rapidly, prices fall, competition increases and the market expands, and the customer has knowledge about the product.

mcqs.question: 'Human resource management' is placed among the support activities of the value chain because it:

options.A: Is managed by a separate department
options.B: Transcends all primary activities
options.C: Is the most expensive activity in most firms
options.D: Does not add value directly

mcqs.explanation: SM §2.4.2: human resource management 'is a particularly important area which transcends all primary activities', covering recruiting, managing, training, developing and rewarding people.

mcqs.question: The study material says a firm's profitability tends to be higher when:

options.A: Other firms are blocked from entering the industry
options.B: Exit barriers are high
options.C: Fixed costs are high
options.D: Products are undifferentiated commodities

mcqs.explanation: SM §2.5.1, threat of new entrants: 'A firm's profitability tends to be higher when other firms are blocked from entering the industry.' The other three options all reduce profitability.

mcqs.question: The study material's four factors from which the experience curve results are:

options.A: Learning effects, economies of scale, product redesign and technological improvements in production
options.B: Capital, scale, differentiation and brand
options.C: Volume, price, cost and margin
options.D: Procurement, technology, human resources and infrastructure

mcqs.explanation: SM §2.5.3 lists exactly these four. Option B is part of the barriers-to-entry list and option D is the value chain's support activities.

mcqs.question: In the value-creation diagram, the gap between the **value to customer** and the **price** is called:

options.A: The firm's margin
options.B: The firm's cost of value creation
options.C: The profitable pricing band
options.D: The customer's surplus

mcqs.explanation: SM §2.5.4 figure: cost of value creation at the bottom, then price, then value to customer; price minus cost is the firm's margin, value minus price is the customer's surplus, and the whole band is the profitable pricing band.

mcqs.question: A business that believes customers will choose the product with the best quality, performance, design or features has which orientation?

options.A: Production orientation
options.B: Product orientation
options.C: Sales orientation
options.D: Customer orientation

mcqs.explanation: SM §2.6: product-oriented businesses think buyers choose products with the best quality, performance, design or features; production-oriented businesses believe customers choose low-price products.

mcqs.question: Which of the following is **not** among the typical variables used to differentiate firms when constructing a strategic group map?

options.A: Degree of vertical integration (none, partial, full)
options.B: Product-line breadth (wide, narrow)
options.C: Degree of service offered (no-frills, limited, full)
options.D: Ratio of debt to equity (low, medium, high)

mcqs.explanation: SM §2.7.1 names six variables: price/quality range; geographic coverage; degree of vertical integration; product-line breadth; use of distribution channels; and degree of service offered. Capital structure is not among them.

mcqs.question: The study material's own illustration of an industry's key success factors is drawn from:

options.A: Apparel manufacturing — appealing designs and colour combinations, and low-cost manufacturing efficiency
options.B: Automobiles — the experience curve at Maruti Suzuki
options.C: Coir — competition from synthetic fibre
options.D: Real estate — the effect of higher interest rates on buyers

mcqs.explanation: SM §2.7.2 uses apparel manufacturing. The other three are genuine illustrations from this chapter but of the experience curve (§2.5.3), the threat of substitutes (§2.5.1) and the economic environment (§2.3.2) respectively.

descriptive.question: In light of the five forces as propagated by Michael Porter, explain the common barriers which may cause restraint for the keenness of new entrepreneurs.
answer_points: Open with the framing: these barriers increase the competitiveness of existing firms and discourage new entrants, impacting industry profitability; barriers to entry are economic forces or 'hurdles' that slow down or impede entry.

**Capital requirements** — firms lacking funds are effectively barred, enhancing incumbents' profitability. **Economies of scale** — the decline in per-unit cost as volume grows lets large firms produce high volumes at successively lower costs.

**Product differentiation** — physical or perceptual differences that make a product special or unique in customers' eyes; the cost of creating genuine differences may be too high for new entrants. **Switching costs** — buyers may have to test a product, negotiate new contracts, train personnel or modify facilities, incurring financial and psychological costs.

**Brand identity** — particularly important for infrequently purchased, high unit cost products; new entrants must commit substantial resources over a long period. **Access to distribution channels** — existing firms often influence channels and can retard or impede their use.
**Possibility of aggressive retaliation** — the mere threat can deter entry; a new firm's launch may lead incumbents to cut prices and raise advertising budgets.

descriptive.question: A manufacturer of home audio systems finds that its sales have plateaued despite heavy promotion, while a rival's new wireless speaker range is growing fast. Identify the product-life-cycle stages involved, and advise the manufacturer on the strategic choices open to it.
answer_points: The firm's own range is in **maturity**: a slowdown in the growth rate, tough competition, a stabilised market and profit coming down because of stiff competition. At this stage organisations have to work for maintaining stability.
The rival's range is in **growth**: rapid market acceptance, with demand expanding rapidly, prices falling, competition increasing and the market expanding.

**The main advantage of the PLC approach** is that it can be used to diagnose a portfolio of products or businesses to establish the stage at which each exists, with particular attention to those in the declining stage.

**Strategic choices:** expansion is feasible for businesses in the introductory and growth stages; mature businesses may be used as sources of cash for investment in other businesses which need resources; a combination of strategies such as selective harvesting and retrenchment may be adopted for declining businesses.

**Advice:** treat the mature range as a cash source and fund entry into the growing wireless segment, so that a balanced portfolio of businesses is built up by exercising strategic choice based on the PLC concept. If the mature range slips into decline — a sharp downward drift as a new product replaces it — diversification or retrenchment follows.

descriptive.question: A hospital group wants to understand the competitive landscape of its city before opening a fourth facility. Explain the steps it should follow and the questions each step answers.
answer_points: Competitive landscape is a business analysis which identifies competitors, either direct or indirect, and permits comprehension of their vision, mission, core values, niche market, strengths and weaknesses; it requires an application of **competitive intelligence**.
**(i) Identify the competitor** — identify the competitors in the industry and have actual data about their respective market share. *Who are the competitors and how big are they?*

**(ii) Understand the competitors** — use market research reports, the internet, newspapers, social media, industry reports and other sources to understand the products and services they offer in different markets. *What are their products and services?*

**(iii) Determine the strengths of the competitors** — what do they do well, and why do customers give them their business? *What are their financial positions? What gives them cost and price advantage? What are they likely to do next? How strong is their distribution network? What are their human resource strengths?*

**(iv) Determine the weaknesses of the competitors** — identified from consumer reports and reviews in various media, and financial weakness from annual reports. *Where are they lacking?* **(v) Put all of the information together** — draw an inference about what they are not offering and what the firm can do to fill in the gaps. *What will the business do with this information? What improvements does the firm need to make? How can the firm exploit the weaknesses of competitors?*

descriptive.question: Explain value creation and the profitable pricing band, and state the two ways in which, according to Michael Porter, a company can generate competitive advantage.
answer_points: **Value creation** is an activity or performance by the firm to create value that increases the worth of goods, services, business processes or even the whole business system. Value is measured by a product's features, quality, availability, durability, performance and services, for which customers are willing to pay; businesses now pursue it both for customers and for stakeholders who want their investment to appreciate.
**Three factors** determine how profitable a company becomes: the value customers place on its products, the price it charges, and the costs of creating those products.

**The profitable pricing band:** the firm's cost of value creation sits at the bottom, the price above it and the value to the customer above that. Price minus cost is the **firm's margin**; value minus price is the **customer's surplus**; the whole band is the **profitable pricing band**. The excess of what a consumer would pay over the price charged is value creation — the consumer values the product or service more than it actually costs them.

**Utility versus price:** the value customers place on a product reflects the utility they get — the happiness or satisfaction gained from consuming or owning it. Utility must be distinguished from price; it is a function of attributes such as performance, design, quality and point-of-sale and after-sale service.

**Porter's two routes:** differentiation — the capability to provide customers superior and special value through special features, quality or after-sales service, allowing a higher price and higher profits provided expenses stay comparable to competitors' costs — or **cost advantage**. Porter used the value chain to explore which organisational functions deliver either, dividing the firm into primary and supporting activities to reveal the potential sources of differentiation and the firm's cost behaviour.

descriptive.question: A food-delivery platform has seen a sudden rise in orders after a festival campaign featuring local chefs. Using the conceptual domains of consumer behaviour, explain what may be driving the change and why understanding it matters.
answer_points: Customer behaviour moves beyond the identification of customers to explain **how they purchase products**, examining shopping frequency, product preferences and the perception of the firm's marketing, sales and service offerings.

**External influences** — advertisement, peer recommendations and social norms — have a direct impact on the psychological and internal processes behind consumer decisions, and divide into **the company's marketing efforts and the numerous environmental elements**. The festival campaign and the chefs' endorsement are both.

**Internal influences** are psychological factors internal to the customer, including **motivation and attitudes**; a festival campaign works on the motive to celebrate and on the perception of authenticity.

**Decision making** — a rational consumer seeks information, integrates it with existing knowledge, weighs advantages and disadvantages and chooses, through problem recognition → search for alternatives → seeking information and weighing pros and cons → final choice. Note the qualification: the full process mostly applies to purchases significant to the customer, such as a car, television or refrigerator, rather than to an impulse food order.

**Post-decision processes** — the final phase is evaluating the outcome: a happy customer may make a repeat purchase and recommend it to others, while a customer with dissonance will neither purchase again nor recommend. **Why it matters:** understanding these behaviours enables businesses to establish effective marketing and advertising campaigns, provide products and services that meet customers' needs, and retain customers for repeat sales.

descriptive.question: "Attractiveness is relative, not absolute." Explain the factors on which a conclusion about industry attractiveness is based, and the strategies that follow for strong and weak participants.
answer_points: Industry analysis culminates in conclusions about the relative attractiveness or unattractiveness of the industry, **both near-term and long-term**; companies invest the promoters' or the public's capital and should be careful in choosing an industry.

**The factors:** growth potential and futuristic viability; whether competition currently permits adequate profitability and whether the forces will strengthen or weaken; whether prevailing driving forces will affect profitability favourably or unfavourably; the firm's own competitive position and whether it will grow stronger or weaker; the potential to capitalise on the vulnerabilities of weaker rivals; the ability to defend against or counteract the unattractive factors; the degrees of risk and uncertainty; the severity of problems facing the industry as a whole; and whether continued participation adds importantly to success in other industries.

**The proposition and its limit:** above-average overall profit prospects make an industry attractive and below-average prospects unattractive; but it is a mistake to think of industries as attractive or unattractive to all firms and all potential entrants — environments unattractive to weak competitors may be attractive to strong ones. A well-entrenched leader in a lacklustre industry can still earn good profitability, while an uphill battle against much stronger rivals can make an otherwise attractive industry unattractive.

**If attractive:** participants employ strategies calculated to strengthen their long-term competitive positions, expanding sales efforts and investing in additional facilities and equipment as needed.

**If unattractive:** more successful participants invest cautiously, look for ways to protect long-term competitiveness and profitability, and perhaps acquire smaller firms if the price is right, with strong companies considering diversification into more attractive businesses over the longer term. **Weak companies in unattractive industries** may merge with a rival to bolster market share and profitability, or begin looking outside the industry for attractive diversification opportunities.

quick.q: State the two major limitations of strategic analysis.
quick.a: It gives many innovative options but does not tell which one to pick; and it can be time-consuming, hurting organisational functioning.

quick.q: Name the five benefits of interaction between a business and its environment.
quick.a: Determine opportunities and threats; give direction for growth; continuous learning; image building; meeting competition.

quick.q: Name the five elements of the macro environment.
What does PESTLE stand for, and what was it before?
quick.a: Political, economic, socio-cultural, technological, legal, environmental. It was PEST before legal and environmental were added.

quick.q: Name the four steps in international strategic planning.
quick.a: Evaluate global opportunities and threats against internal capabilities; describe the scope of global operations; create global business objectives; develop distinct corporate strategies.

quick.q: Name the five characteristics of business products.
quick.a: Tangible or intangible; has a price; features that deliver satisfaction; pivotal for business; has a useful life.

quick.q: Name the five primary and four support activities of the value chain.
quick.a: Primary: inbound logistics, operations, outbound logistics, marketing and sales, service. Support: procurement, technology development, human resource management, infrastructure.

quick.q: Name the seven barriers to entry.
quick.a: Capital requirements, economies of scale, product differentiation, switching costs, brand identity, access to distribution channels, possibility of aggressive retaliation.

quick.q: Name the six conditions in which rivalry becomes cut-throat.
quick.a: Industry leader, number of competitors, high fixed costs, exit barriers, lack of product differentiation, slow growth.

quick.q: Name the five steps to understand the competitive landscape.
quick.a: Identify the competitor; understand the competitors; determine their strengths; determine their weaknesses; put all of the information together.

quick.q: Name the four steps of strategic group mapping.
quick.a: Identify the differentiating competitive characteristics; plot firms on a two-variable map; assign firms in the same strategy space to the same group; draw circles proportional to each group's share of total industry sales revenues.

quick.q: Name the three questions that identify an industry's KSFs.
quick.a: On what basis do customers choose between competing brands (and which product attributes are crucial to sales)? What resources and competitive capabilities does a seller need? What does it take to achieve a sustainable competitive advantage?

true_false.q: Competitors are part of the macro environment.
true_false.a: False. The study material lists suppliers, consumers, marketing intermediaries and competitors under the **micro** environment, because they act directly and regularly.

true_false.q: Profitability tends to be higher in industries with high exit barriers.
true_false.a: False. Profitability tends to be higher in industries with **few** exit barriers, because rivalry declines when competitors can leave.

true_false.q: The strategic-management process is fundamentally different for a global firm.
true_false.a: False. It is essentially the same, but much more complicated due to additional variables and linkages.

true_false.q: The study material says the conceptual domains of consumer behaviour are three in number.
true_false.a: Partly. The sentence says three but the list that follows has four headings — external influences, internal influences, decision making and post-decision processes — and ICAI's own January 2026 answer calls them four. Write four.

true_false.q: A customer and a consumer always mean the same person.
true_false.a: False. A customer is the purchaser and may exist as a consumer or only as a customer; the parent who buys groceries for the family is the customer, the family are the consumers.

true_false.q: Value chain analysis began as a tool of competitive strategy.
true_false.a: False. It was originally introduced as an **accounting analysis** of the value added of separate steps in complex manufacturing processes; Porter later linked it to competitive advantage.

The force represented by coir's displacement by synthetic fibre.
The company ICAI cites for the experience curve in the Indian automobile industry.

right: The experience curve phenomenon in the contemporary Indian automobile industry
Environmental analysis is the process by which strategists monitor the economic, governmental/legal, market/competitive, supplier/technological, geographic and social settings
The most important environmental factors are socio-economic, technological, supplier, competitors and government
The analysis is the critical starting point of strategic thinking
The five forces, the value chain, and differentiation or cost advantage as the two routes to competitive advantage

differentiate.a: Micro is the immediate periphery — suppliers, consumers, marketing intermediaries, competitors — influencing the firm directly and regularly. Macro significantly affects operations but is typically beyond the firm's direct control and influence.

differentiate.q: Competitive landscape vs Porter's five forces
differentiate.a: The landscape identifies and understands named rivals in five steps and ends in the gaps the firm can fill. The five forces diagnose industry-wide competitive pressure in three steps and end in a judgement on whether attractive profits are available.

Customer analysis identifies target clients and determines their wants through surveys, data, positioning evaluation, profiles and segmentation. Customer behaviour explains how they purchase — shopping frequency, preferences and perception — through four conceptual domains.

differentiate.q: Experience curve vs economies of scale
differentiate.a: Economies of scale are the decline in per-unit cost as volume grows, and are one of four causes of the experience curve. The experience curve is the wider phenomenon that unit costs fall with **cumulative** volume, also through learning effects, product redesign and technological improvements.

Utility is what customers get from a product — the happiness or satisfaction of consuming or owning it, a function of performance, design, quality and service. Price is what the company charges. The study material insists the two must be distinguished.

sections.title: Strategic analysis
points: Judgments must flow directly from analysis of the external environment and internal resources
Two situational considerations: industry and competitive conditions; own capabilities and market position
Two limitations: many options, no choice rule; time-consuming
Three issues: strategy evolves; balance of external and internal; risk (external/internal × short/long)
External analysis: customer, competitor, market, environmental. Internal: performance, determinants

sections.title: Business environment
points: All external factors, influences or situations affecting business decisions, plans and operations
Five benefits of interaction: opportunities and threats, growth direction, learning, image, competition
Micro: suppliers, consumers, intermediaries, competitors — direct and regular
Macro: economic, socio-cultural, technological, political, legal — beyond direct control

sections.title: Macro elements and PESTLE
points: Demographic (characteristics) vs socio-cultural (behaviour and beliefs)
Economic determines the strength and size of the market
Political-legal: partly general, partly specific; Make in India, Aatmanirbhar Bharat, PLI
Technology is opportunity and threat at once; AI, ML, RPA
PESTLE: six factors, was PEST; encourages proactive and structured thinking

sections.title: Going global
points: Global business: common ownership, common pool of resources, common strategy
Four steps: evaluate, scope, objectives, strategies
Reasons: growth, shrinking distance, inadequate domestic markets, resources, transport costs, foreign market expansion, services and regional integration, collapsing trade barriers, alliances
Three levels of assessment: multinational, regional, country

sections.title: Product, PLC and value chain
points: Five characteristics: tangible/intangible, price, features, pivotal, useful life
PLC: introduction, growth, maturity, decline; diagnose a portfolio; expansion, cash source, harvest/retrench
Primary: inbound logistics, operations, outbound logistics, marketing and sales, service
Support: procurement (processes, not resources), technology development, HRM (transcends all), infrastructure

sections.title: Industry and the five forces
points: Goal: estimate competitive pressure now and in the near future
Three steps: identify, rate (fierce/strong/moderate/weak), judge collective strength
Seven barriers: capital, scale, differentiation, switching costs, brand, channels, retaliation
Buyer power: knowledge, big buyers, product not critical and buyers concentrated
Supplier power: crucial with no substitutes, high switching costs, more concentrated
Cut-throat rivalry: leader, number, fixed costs, exit barriers, no differentiation, slow growth
Substitutes: latent, sudden, same or nearly the same function

sections.title: Attractiveness, experience, value
points: Attractiveness: near-term and long-term; nine factors; relative, not absolute
Attractive → expand; unattractive and strong → invest cautiously, buy small firms cheap; unattractive and weak → merge or leave
Experience curve: unit costs fall with cumulative volume; 'we learn as we grow'; four causes; a key barrier to entry; Maruti Suzuki
Value creation: cost → price → value; margin and customer's surplus; three profitability factors; utility ≠ price; differentiation or cost advantage

sections.title: Market, customer and competition
points: Market is a place; marketing is the activity; four Ps = product, place, pricing, promotion
Four orientations: product, production, sales, customer
Customer purchases; consumer consumes
Customer analysis: surveys, data, positioning, profiles, segmentation
Customer behaviour: external, internal, decision making (problem → search → seek → choose), post-decision (repeat or dissonance)
Competitive strategy: how to compete; create and protect advantage; more profitable in the long run
Landscape: five steps + strategic group mapping's four; KSFs: three questions, three or four factors only
